title: Leaders Who Take More Than Their Fair Share
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article examines leaders who claim outsized resources or privileges for themselves and the psychological mechanism, Motivated Reasoning, that lets them justify it. Such leaders convince themselves their extra share is earned and that others either won't notice or won't be hurt by it. The author identifies two organizational conditions that enable this behavior: a lack of transparency around how leaders benefit, and ambiguity about what's actually acceptable. Elevated status compounds the problem, since leaders who feel exalted often reason their position entitles them to more. The piece argues good organizations treat this as a systems problem rather than a character flaw, closing the gaps in clarity and transparency and avoiding cultures that turn top performers into untouchable stars.
points: Self-serving leaders use Motivated Reasoning to justify taking more than their fair share
Lack of transparency and ambiguity about acceptable behavior both enable selfish decisions
Elevated status leads some leaders to feel entitled to extra privileges
Good organizations reduce this behavior through clarity and transparency, treating bad actors as made, not born
quotes: They make the conscious decision to help themselves to resources, perquisites, and financial gains, sometimes at the expense of others.
With what psychologists call Motivated Reasoning, these self-serving leaders seek and acquire information that is consistent with their end goals and desires.
When it is unclear what leaders are allowed to do, some leaders will take advantage of this vagueness and do as they please.
Status also plays a large role in encouraging selfish behavior.

Good organizations understand that bad actors who acquire extra privileges are made, not born, and they do everything in their power to make it harder for them to take liberties with organizational resources.
No selfish leader ever thinks of themselves as selfish. Instead, they reason their way to self-serving choices that meet their personal goals and desires.
